speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is advisable in considering a resolution of this kind that we have as widely representative a viewpoint as possible. The last occasion parliament had a chance to review the activities of the federal district commission in connection with the national capital plan was in* 1944, at which time considerable interest was generated throughout the country in the prospect of a place of beauty, a city of beauty, arising here in Ottawa.

However, since that time there has been no direct discussion of the matter by a committee, and I have the feeling that Canadians living in provinces more remote from Ontario and Quebec are somewhat out of touch with the developments which have taken place following the plan laid down during the sessions of the committee in 1944. At that time, I recall, looking at the problem from the viewpoint of an outsider, there was considerable interest generated. However, more recently, I am afraid, in other parts of the country the general public has not been keeping in touch with the developments taking place.
I first had the opportunity to visit the capital in 1942. Like most Canadians who come to Ottawa for the first time, my first reaction was that of disappointment. We tend to regard the capital of any nation as a place of beauty, a show place to a certain extent, because of the peculiar position it occupies in the affairs of the country. Unfortunately, because of the lateness in starting to plan our capital city on an organized basis, up to the present time Ottawa, like most of our Canadian cities, has just grown. There has been no organization of any kind. Fortunately during recent years, since the committee of 1944, there is some obvious evidence that the plans laid down on that occasion are at long last beginning to take shape.
Ottawa is also in the fortunate position that it has one of the best possible natural locations for a capital city. In 1942, when I viewed the city for the first time, I did so from what might be called the bird's eye view, from the air. Being connected with the air force at Uplands airport at the time I had a chance to fly over this area quite regularly, and from that perspective the district surrounding our capital city certainly appears one of extreme natural beauty. Any of the deficiencies that are criticized by visitors to Ottawa from more remote parts of the country are the result of delay in development and the unplanned growth of the city since it was first chosen to be capital of this young country. The nature of the early commercial activities, of course, has added some eyesores to the surrounding district which are only gradually being eliminated.
It was more by accident than by good judgment that the most attractive feature of the city at the present time, the federal district commission driveway, associated closely with the Rideau canal, grew out of that early defence measure Colonel By took in the years Canada was under threat of attack from our neighbour to the south. That has now become a central feature of the city and is one part 67509-121
National Capital Plan
of the capital that we can show to visitors with a great deal of pride.
As we come to the activities of the committee about to be set up, there are one or two suggestions I have in mind that I think should be drawn to the attention of those who have the privilege of serving on the committee. It has been pointed out already in this discussion that the original intention of the planners who first began to think in terms of a more rationalized development of our capital city was to pattern it after the city of Washington, the capital of the United States. As I see the development taking place, particularly in reference to buildings already constructed by the Department of Public Works, I get the feeling that the pattern in that regard is almost too close. The buildings that have already appeared on Wellington street, for example, seem to suggest that we are going to emphasize heavy stone types of structures reminiscent of an architectural age that is now some 200 or 300 years in the past.
I have not examined this question in any detail at all, nor am I any authority on architecture, but the general impression from casual observation is that the emphasis in our public buildings in this downtown area is going to be on huge monuments of stone. Maybe it is a deliberate attempt to reconstruct in Canada the equivalent of Constitution avenue in the city of Washington, D.C., but it seems to me the reverse of the architectural trend that is under way on this continent, where the emphasis in recent years has been on less ponderous structures designed for utilitarian, functional purposes, where the emphasis is not on the appearance of grandeur but rather on the suitability as work areas.
Most of these buildings are going to be occupied by civil servants. I take as a concrete example of this new modernistic trend the sort of structure that you see in the United Nations building, with emphasis on accessibility, surrounded by grassed areas, with a considerable part of the building devoted to window space. The United Nations secretariat building is often referred to as the glass house, mainly because at a distance the walls appear to be entirely constructed of glass.
As I have pointed out at the commencement of these observations, Canada has delayed somewhat long in coming to grips with this problem of building a capital worthy of the nation. That has had certain disadvantages, which have been outlined. We have seen a city grow up around parliament hill that has all the undesirable aspects

National Capital Plan
of the rapid growth of our modern cities, but it has this advantage. We are now in a position to start from scratch, as it were, so far as the architectural features of our capital plans are concerned. It would seem from a common sense standpoint much more desirable to project our thinking into the future and try to gear our architectural developments to the future, rather than tie them into the past.
It might be true that a certain atmosphere of grandeur is required in order to provide the necessary stately avenues for ceremonial and state occasions. But if we are thinking in terms of the era of capital city develop' ment of two or three hundred years ago; if we are trying to recreate here the atmosphere of some of the European capitals, I feel that we are decidedly out of touch with the general atmosphere of a country such as Canada, where there is a certain degree of modesty surrounding the living habits of the people as a whole. That is the main point I want to make in this discussion.
I have one final suggestion I should like to put before the house. The sittings of the committee will provide another occasion to arouse the general interest of the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other. I suggest that we use every possible opportunity by means of television, radio, every form of mass media communication that we have today, to bring the results of the deliberations of the committee before the people of Canada, and to bring before the people of Canada such outstanding events as the annual tulip festival. Only by so doing can we create the sentiment right across the country that will draw the attention of every Canadian citizen to the importance of the comprehensive development of our capital city.
In view of some of the difficulties that have been outlined with respect to the relationships between the various levels of government in trying to come to a coordinated agreement on national capital development, if there is no other solution whereby closer co-ordination can be maintained perhaps it would be advisable for this purpose to have a committee of this type sit more frequently so that we will be assured of a capital city, a capital area, worthy of a nation occupying the position that Canada does in the modern world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add one or two brief remarks and relate them chiefly to some of the things said by the Leader of the Opposition. I read in the resolution that a joint committee is to be set up, and so on, to

review and report upon "the progress and programs in developing and implementing the plan for the national capital". The Leader of the Opposition spoke at considerable length about the physical aspects of this development. He spoke about streets and bridges and all the necessary things which enter into a plan, but the point I wish to refer to and which he stressed greatly is what one might call the cultural side of the matter.
He referred to a national theatre and the national gallery. I want to mention that for this reason. It seems to me that the communists are facing us with an entirely new threat, and it is in a sense not a physical but an educational threat. They are making us apprehensive lest, unless we distort our education, unless we stress technical education almost wholly, we may be left behind and one day find ourselves faced with overwhelming threats in the economic world.
It is for that reason that I wish to emphasize what the Leader of the Opposition said. I think there is a danger in our country that we may become not only exhilarated but even fascinated by our material progress. That is natural and inevitable, and I think healthy too, but on the other hand it does mean that we need to be called back, so to speak, from time to time to consider these other aspects of life. Therefore I was glad that the Leader of the Opposition spent a good deal of time not merely talking about the mechanical processes of our day to day lives but speaking about the art of living. By that I mean, of course, literature, painting and all the other things that go with it. When we look back we do know that in ancient days there were cities that have left their mark ever since. The city of Athens 2,500 years ago was, I suppose, about the same size as Ottawa, and it has influenced the whole world by the literary and artistic legacies it has left.
So I venture to express the hope that the committee in considering its work may feel there is a wonderful opportunity here in Ottawa for a lead to be given, and what an opportunity we have in this country, a kind of double opportunity because we have two great cultures. It seems to me that the committee would do well to consider its responsibilities in that direction. We are prospering greatly. We read almost fabulous figures of our material progress, and I hope that in the consideration of those we will not be lead to disregard these other things.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say a brief word in regard to the setting up of this committee. The committee which has been doing such excellent work during the past two sessions should be congratulated on the wide range of knowledge they have obtained from a large field of experts. The calling of those experts has resulted in some very interesting evidence which I believe should be studied not only by all members of this parliament but by the people of Canada as a whole. I believe any person in Canada-at least the vast majority of us-would gain a great deal by reading the evidence of this committee and learning something about modern trends and about the history of capital punishment within our own country.
Among the names of those called before the committee is that of Mr. J. V. Fornataro, director of corrections. I refer also to the evidence given by Professor C. W. Topping, who is professor of sociology at United College, Winnipeg, Manitoba. We find the name of such a man as Mr. J. Alex. Edmison, Q.C., assistant to the principal, Queen's University, and who is director of American Prison Association and also a member of the special committee of the Department of Justice to study remission and parole; Mr. Virgil W. Peterson, operator of the Chicago science commission. The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police gave evidence. This association in their brief, I note, state they could almost agree with Professor Sellin that there is a trend away from capital punishment these days and that it will disappear in all countries of western culture in the near future.
The general consensus of opinion, I would say, expressed by these experts supported the idea that capital punishment should be done away with. People interested would be surprised to learn that capital punishment has not served as a deterrent to the committing of murder. In the evidence given by Mr. Fornataro he stated emphatically that he was against capital punishment, and that sufficiently significant changes had occurred in today's understanding of behaviour since the original framing of the Criminal Code in Canada which would lead us to the conclusion that the very purpose of our system of justice should be redefined. It is a study of great interest, a matter of public concern across Canada. He states this-

speechtext:
I am pleased to have those remarks from the hon. member for Timis-kaming. It is because I was not a member of that committee last year, and because I am looking forward to being a member of that committee this year-I have already been named on it-that I was referring to some of the material which I found in reading the evidence which was presented.
If the hon. member had been in the chamber when I began my remarks she would have heard me state that the committee was to be commended for the great work it has done. It was my opinion, on reading the evidence, that the majority of those giving evidence, from their knowledge and scientific study of the matter, were generally opposed to capital punishment. It was not my intention to influence anybody in that regard. I was merely making the suggestion that every member of this house should read that evidence and should make himself as familiar as possible with the information that has been given to us. I think it is most valuable.
I merely made that suggestion to the house. After all, we cannot ignore the verdict of history which rapidly leads us to the conclusion that crime has seemed to flourish most widely in times and in places where the punishment was most rigorous. If you look at the evidence heard during the past two years, I think by and large you will find that it will support that contention.
As an example, it might be of interest to the members of this house to know that just a little over 100 years ago history records the fact that a lad by the name of Nicholas White, a boy of 9 years of age, was sentenced to death at Old Bailey in England for stealing two pennyworth of paint. It would indicate that we have come a long way. It would also indicate that we should continue our study and make it a matter of law in this country that in the punishment of crime we see that we are doing the thing which we expect punishment to do.

I was surprised to learn that the evidence against hanging was that it did not deter. I think one of the strongest arguments that were used against capital punishment-this is how I feel myself, and I approach this with an open mind-is that there has been evidence that people have been hanged, and then some years afterwards it was discovered that they were innocent. As someone has said, hanging is so permanent. To whom can one appeal for justice when such a thing occurs, and when the state has carried out the punishment for a crime which he did not commit?
Speaking of the kind of evidence that might be given and the effort that might be made under such circumstances, Professor Topping said this. He was indicating his belief that capital punishment was discriminatory. He said:
When a man is battling for his life he will exert his full force and he will draw upon all his resources and the resources of his friends. Specifically this means that he will employ the best counsel possible, even at a fee of $20,000, and that he will rally what friends he has to his assistance. This counsel and these friends will use their best skill to avoid so severe a penalty as death. Legal knowledge, psychology, and experience will be drawn upon. Since the evidence is likely to be circumstantial and based on the principles of logic, conviction is difficult. Murder is a low-visibility crime with few eye witnesses who can be called in to testify at the trial. With powerful friends and resources the struggle will be a long one; no quarter will be asked or given. And there may be delays until the furore has died down; and appeals.
